stem: The `City` field has both Cologne and Köln as separate members, and the analyst wants them to count as one city in the view. Which action does this?

options.text: Right-click the `City` field and choose Create Hierarchy
options.rationale: A hierarchy stacks fields for drilling. It does not merge members of one field.

options.text: Select both marks and choose Create Set to build an In/Out field
options.rationale: A set only marks members as In or Out. Both spellings would still be separate members.

options.text: Select both city headers and click the group icon
options.rationale: The group icon combines the selected members into a single group, which is what merging spellings needs.

options.text: Drag `City` to the Filters shelf and keep only Köln
options.rationale: Filtering removes the Cologne rows rather than combining them with Köln.

explanation: A group combines related members of one field into a single member. You can start one from selected marks or headers, using the paperclip group icon on the tooltip or the toolbar.

stem: Which Data pane menu path starts a group on a dimension?

options.text: Right-click the field, then Create > Group
options.rationale: In the Data pane, Create > Group opens the dialog where you pick the members to combine.

options.text: Right-click the field, then Create > Set
options.rationale: Create > Set opens the set dialog, which defines an In/Out subset and combines nothing.

options.text: Right-click the field, then Create Hierarchy
options.rationale: Create Hierarchy starts a drill path of several fields; it doesn't combine members.

options.text: Right-click the field, then Show Filter
options.rationale: Show Filter adds a filter card to the sheet and does not create any new field.

explanation: Groups can be created from marks or headers in the view or from the Data pane. In the Data pane you right-click a dimension, choose Create > Group, then select the members to combine.

stem: An analyst selects the `Comedy` and `Drama` headers and clicks the group icon without naming anything. What name does the group get?

options.text: It stays unnamed until the analyst opens Edit Group and types a name
options.rationale: A default name is created automatically, so the group is never unnamed.

options.text: It is named `Group 1`, and the name cannot be changed afterwards
options.rationale: The default name comes from the member names, and the group can be renamed.

options.text: It takes the name of the field, such as `Genre (group)`, and the members are hidden
options.rationale: The default name uses the combined member names, and the members are not hidden by naming.

options.text: A default name built from the combined member names, which Rename can change
options.rationale: Tableau generates the name from the members. Rename lets you replace it with something clearer.

explanation: When you group, Tableau names the group by joining the member names. Use Rename in the dialog to give it a better name.

stem: The Driftlight content team created a genre group last month and now wants to move one genre out of it. Where do they do that?

options.text: Right-click the group in the Data pane, choose Create Set, and untick the member
options.rationale: Create Set builds a new In/Out field and leaves the group itself unchanged.

options.text: Choose Edit Group on the group field, select the member and click Ungroup
options.rationale: Edit Group is where you select members and click Ungroup to take them out of the group.

options.text: Drag the group field onto another field in the Data pane
options.rationale: Dropping a field onto another creates a hierarchy and does not change group membership.

options.text: Open the Filters shelf, edit the group's filter and exclude the member
options.rationale: A filter hides the member from the view. It does not take it out of the group definition.

explanation: Existing groups are edited through the group field's Edit Group command. There you select members and click Ungroup, or rename the group.

stem: The content team wants three named genre groups, with every remaining genre lumped into one bucket. Which setting does this?

options.text: Include 'Other' in the Edit Group dialog
options.rationale: Include 'Other' groups all remaining, non-grouped members into an Other group.

options.text: Show In/Out of Set on the Color shelf
options.rationale: Show In/Out of Set belongs to sets, and it gives two categories, not named groups.

options.text: Add the remaining genres to a context filter
options.rationale: A context filter removes rows from the view. The leftovers would disappear and not be bucketed.

options.text: Create a hierarchy with `Genre` at the top level
options.rationale: A hierarchy adds drill levels and does not collect leftover members.

explanation: Include 'Other' keeps a few named groups and puts the long tail of members into one extra group. It is useful when most members are not worth showing individually.

stem: Which statement describes a group in Tableau?

options.text: It splits a dimension into In and Out members based on a subset
options.rationale: That describes a set, which marks each member as In or Out.

options.text: It stacks related dimensions so the view can be drilled down and up
options.rationale: That describes a hierarchy, which uses the + and - icons to drill.

options.text: It combines members of a field into larger categories
options.rationale: A group merges members, such as several genres into one broader category.

options.text: It removes marks from the view by testing a condition on a measure
options.rationale: That describes a filter. A group changes how members are categorized and removes none.

explanation: Groups, sets and hierarchies are easy to mix up. A group merges members into new categories, a set marks In or Out, and a hierarchy orders dimensions for drilling.

stem: Which two actions start the creation of a group? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: Drag a dimension onto another dimension in the Data pane
options.rationale: This starts a hierarchy, not a group.

options.text: Select marks in the view and click the group icon on the tooltip
options.rationale: The tooltip's paperclip icon groups the selected marks.

options.text: Right-click a mark and choose Create Set
options.rationale: This makes a set with In and Out members.

options.text: Right-click a dimension in the Data pane and choose Create > Group
options.rationale: This opens the group dialog from the Data pane.

options.text: Drag a dimension to the Filters shelf
options.rationale: This opens the Filter dialog and creates no group.

explanation: You can create a group from selected marks or headers in the view, or from a dimension in the Data pane. The other actions create a hierarchy, a set or a filter.

stem: Which two things can an analyst do in the Edit Group dialog? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: Select members and click Ungroup
options.rationale: Ungroup takes the selected members out of the group.

options.text: Define the members by a Top N rule on a measure
options.rationale: Top rules belong to the dynamic set dialog, not to groups.

options.text: Switch the group to a fixed or dynamic type
options.rationale: Groups have no fixed or dynamic type. That distinction applies to sets.

options.text: Add the group to a context filter so it runs first
options.rationale: Context is set from a filter's menu and is not an option in the group dialog.

options.text: Include 'Other' to collect the non-grouped members
options.rationale: This option puts the remaining members into an Other group.

explanation: Edit Group lets you rename the group, ungroup members and include an Other group for the rest. Rules based on measures belong to sets and filters.

stem: Which two Driftlight requests call for a group? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: Flag the top 20 titles by minutes watched against all the others
options.rationale: An In/Out flag defined by a Top rule is a set.

options.text: Drill from Type down to Genre in the same view
options.rationale: Drill paths are built with a hierarchy.

options.text: Combine the München and Munich spellings into one city
options.rationale: Merging several members into one category is a group.

options.text: Bundle genres into a Scripted and an Unscripted category
options.rationale: Broader categories made from members are groups.

options.text: Show only sessions that started on a TV
options.rationale: Restricting rows is a filter, not a group.

explanation: A group merges members into new categories. Flagging members In or Out is a set, drilling is a hierarchy, and removing rows is a filter.

stem: An analyst selects five title marks in a bar chart and wants to save exactly those titles as a subset. What should they do?

options.text: Click the group icon on the tooltip and rename the group
options.rationale: A group merges the five titles into one member, which hides them individually.

options.text: Drag `Title` onto `Genre` in the Data pane and name it
options.rationale: This builds a hierarchy of two fields, not a subset.

options.text: Choose Keep Only, then Add to Context on the filter
options.rationale: Keep Only filters the view and does not leave a reusable In/Out field.

options.text: Right-click the marks and choose Create Set
options.rationale: Creating a set from marks gives a fixed set made of the selected members.

explanation: Sets are made from marks with Create Set. The set holds the selected members, and each other member of the field is Out of the set.

stem: Marketing wants a set of the top 20 titles by minutes that updates each week as viewing changes. How is it built?

options.text: Select the top 20 title marks in a bar chart and choose Create Set
options.rationale: A set made from selected marks is fixed and never updates.

options.text: Use Create > Set on `Title` and define it on the Top tab
options.rationale: A set defined on the Top tab is dynamic, so it follows the data.

options.text: Select the top 20 titles and group them with the paperclip icon
options.rationale: A group merges the titles into one member and does not follow the data.

options.text: Drag `Title` onto `Minutes Watched` in the Data pane
options.rationale: Dropping a field onto another does not build a set.

explanation: Dynamic sets are created from a dimension in the Data pane and defined by the General, Condition or Top tab. Condition and Top rules are recomputed when the underlying data changes.

stem: A set was created by selecting marks. Later, new sessions are added to the data. What happens to the set?

options.text: Its members stay exactly as they were selected
options.rationale: A set made from marks is fixed, so its members do not change when the data does.

options.text: It recalculates its members from the new data
options.rationale: Only dynamic sets, defined by a condition or a top N, recalculate.

options.text: It becomes a group made of the selected members
options.rationale: Sets and groups are different fields, and a set never converts into a group.

options.text: It is deleted and has to be created again from the new marks
options.rationale: Fixed sets persist as fields in the Data pane.

explanation: A fixed set keeps the members chosen at creation. A dynamic set follows the data because it is defined by a rule instead of a list of marks.

stem: The analyst wants a set of every title where `SUM(Minutes Watched)` is above a threshold. Which tab of the set dialog defines this?

options.text: General
options.rationale: General is for picking individual members from a list, or Use all.

options.text: Top
options.rationale: Top limits members to a number or a percentage by a measure, not to a threshold.

options.text: Condition
options.rationale: The Condition tab defines a rule on a measure that decides which members are included.

options.text: Fixed
options.rationale: The set dialog has no Fixed tab. A fixed set is the kind made from marks.

explanation: The dynamic set dialog has General, Condition and Top tabs. A threshold such as `SUM(Minutes Watched) > 20000` is a Condition. A limit like the top 10 is a Top definition.

stem: A set named `Top Titles` is on the Color shelf, and the analyst wants only two colors: titles in the set and everything else. What should they choose?

options.text: Right-click the set and choose Create Hierarchy
options.rationale: Hierarchies are built from fields dropped on each other, not from a set.

options.text: Right-click the set and choose Include 'Other'
options.rationale: Include 'Other' belongs to the group dialog.

options.text: Right-click the set and choose Show Members in Set
options.rationale: This lists every member individually, so there would be many colors.

options.text: Right-click the set and choose Show In/Out of Set
options.rationale: This aggregates the members into In and Out categories.

explanation: A set in the view can show its members or collapse them into In and Out. Show In/Out of Set compares the subset against the rest.

stem: Which statement about creating sets is correct?

options.text: A set from the Data pane can use several dimensions, and one from marks only one
options.rationale: This is reversed. Marks can span dimensions and the Data pane route cannot.

options.text: A set from marks can use several dimensions, and one from the Data pane uses a single dimension
options.rationale: Marks may carry several dimensions, while the Data pane route works on one dimension.

options.text: Both ways create dynamic sets that update when the underlying data changes
options.rationale: Only the Data pane route, with a Condition or Top rule, gives a dynamic set.

options.text: Both ways create fixed sets whose members are chosen from a list of marks
options.rationale: The Data pane route offers dynamic definitions as well, through the General, Condition and Top tabs.

explanation: Marks give you fixed sets that can cover several dimensions. The Data pane route works on one dimension at a time and can be dynamic.

stem: The analyst selects some marks and wants the set to hold every member except those marks. What helps?

options.text: Choose Exclude these members instead
options.rationale: This option defines the set as everything except the selected members.

options.text: Choose Show In/Out of Set after dragging the set to the Rows shelf
options.rationale: This only changes how a set is displayed after it exists.

options.text: Use Keep Only on the selected marks, which filters the view
options.rationale: Keep Only filters the view and creates no set.

options.text: Create a group from the selected marks and tick Include 'Other'
options.rationale: A group merges members, so it cannot produce an exclusion set.

explanation: The Create Set dialog lets you invert the selection with Exclude these members instead. The result is still a fixed set.

stem: Which two statements describe a dynamic set? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: It is defined on the General, Condition or Top tab
options.rationale: These tabs are the three ways to define it.

options.text: It is created by right-clicking marks and choosing Create Set
options.rationale: That route creates a fixed set.

options.text: It always spans several dimensions
options.rationale: A dynamic set from the Data pane is based on a single dimension.

options.text: Its members change when the underlying data changes
options.rationale: This is what makes it dynamic.

options.text: Its members never change once it exists
options.rationale: That is the behavior of a fixed set.

explanation: Dynamic sets are defined by rules instead of a hand-picked list, so they follow the data. They come from the Data pane and are based on one dimension.

stem: Which two Driftlight requests call for a set? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: Merge Cologne and Köln into one city
options.rationale: Merging members is a group.

options.text: Compare the top 20 titles by minutes with every other title
options.rationale: An In/Out split by a Top rule is a dynamic set.

options.text: Drill from Type down to Genre
options.rationale: Drilling uses a hierarchy.

options.text: Let viewers pick a Device from a card
options.rationale: A filter card is Show Filter, not a set.

options.text: Flag titles where `SUM(Minutes Watched)` exceeds a threshold
options.rationale: A rule on a measure is a Condition on a set.

explanation: A set divides a dimension into In and Out, which makes comparisons of a subset against the rest simple. Merging, drilling and filter cards use other tools.

stem: Where does the analyst start in the Data pane to create a hierarchy from `Type` and `Genre`?

options.text: Right-click `Type` and choose Create > Group, then add `Genre`
options.rationale: Create > Group merges members of one field and does not link two fields.

options.text: Right-click `Type` and choose Create > Set, then add `Genre`
options.rationale: A set marks members of one dimension as In or Out and cannot nest fields.

options.text: Drop `Genre` directly on `Type`, then name the hierarchy
options.rationale: Dropping a field on another creates the hierarchy and prompts for a name.

options.text: Drag both fields to the Filters shelf at the same time
options.rationale: The Filters shelf removes data and builds no drill path.

explanation: A hierarchy is created in the Data pane by dropping one field on top of another. Add the further fields in order from general to detailed.

stem: A dimension sits inside a folder in the Data pane. How can the analyst start a hierarchy from it?

options.text: Right-click the field and select Create > Group
options.rationale: This merges members rather than ordering fields.

options.text: Right-click the field and select Show Filter
options.rationale: This adds a filter card and creates no field.

options.text: Drag the folder onto the Rows shelf and click + on it
options.rationale: Folders are not hierarchies, and + only drills one that already exists.

options.text: Right-click the field and select Create Hierarchy
options.rationale: For a field inside a folder, Create Hierarchy is on its right-click menu.

explanation: Dragging one field onto another is one way to build a hierarchy. For a field inside a folder, the right-click Create Hierarchy command is the alternative.

stem: Which two steps are part of creating a hierarchy in the Data pane? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: Select two marks and click the paperclip group icon
options.rationale: This creates a group of members.

options.text: Right-click a mark and choose Create Set
options.rationale: This creates a set from the mark.

options.text: Drop one field directly on top of another and name the hierarchy
options.rationale: This starts the hierarchy and gives it a name.

options.text: Drag further fields in, ordered from general to detailed
options.rationale: The order sets the drill path, such as Type before Genre.

options.text: Drag the dimension to the Filters shelf
options.rationale: This opens a filter dialog and builds no hierarchy.

explanation: Creating a hierarchy means stacking dimensions in the Data pane, from the most general at the top to the most detailed. In the view, + and - on the hierarchy field then drill down and up.

stem: The analyst has a `Type` › `Genre` hierarchy in the Rows shelf. What does clicking the + icon on the hierarchy field do?

options.text: It adds the hierarchy to the Filters shelf as a context filter.
options.rationale: Filters are added by dragging a field to the Filters shelf, not through the hierarchy icons.

options.text: It drills down, adding the next field as nested headers.
options.rationale: The + icon expands the hierarchy by one level, so the Genre headers nest inside each Type.

options.text: It collapses the view back to the top level of the hierarchy.
options.rationale: Collapsing is the job of the - icon, the opposite of +.

options.text: It converts the hierarchy into a set of In and Out members.
options.rationale: Sets are created with Create Set or Create > Set, not from a hierarchy icon.

explanation: Clicking + on a hierarchy field drills down: the next field in the hierarchy appears as nested headers. Clicking - drills back up.

stem: In which order should an analyst drag fields into a new hierarchy?

options.text: From detailed to general, so the finest field is at the top of the hierarchy.
options.rationale: The top of the hierarchy should be the most general field, because drilling adds detail below it.

options.text: In alphabetical order of the field names, whatever the fields mean.
options.rationale: The order sets the drill path, so it follows meaning, not the alphabet.

options.text: Measures first, then dimensions, so the numbers are at the top level.
options.rationale: A hierarchy stacks dimensions; measures are not part of it.

options.text: From general to detailed, such as `Type`, then `Genre`, then `Sub-Genre`.
options.rationale: The top level comes first, and each field below it adds more detail.

explanation: A hierarchy is a drill path. Drag fields into it from the most general to the most detailed, so that each + click adds a finer level.

stem: The catalogue team has drilled the title hierarchy down to `Sub-Genre` and now wants to return to the `Genre` level. What should they do?

options.text: Delete the hierarchy from the Data pane and build it again from scratch.
options.rationale: Removing the hierarchy is not needed to move up a level; the icons do that.

options.text: Click the + icon on the hierarchy field a second time to undo the first drill.
options.rationale: The + icon drills further down; it never moves back up.

options.text: Click the - icon on the hierarchy field in the view.
options.rationale: The - icon drills up one level, which is the reverse of the + icon.

options.text: Select the headers and choose Exclude to hide the `Sub-Genre` level.
options.rationale: Exclude removes the selected members from the view; it does not drill up a level.

explanation: The + and - icons on a hierarchy field move down and up the levels. Nothing has to be rebuilt to change the level of detail.

stem: Which two statements about hierarchies are true? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: A hierarchy lets the analyst drill from a general level to a more detailed one.
options.rationale: That is what a hierarchy is for.

options.text: A hierarchy merges several members of one field into a single new category.
options.rationale: That describes a group, not a hierarchy.

options.text: A hierarchy splits the members of a dimension into In and Out.
options.rationale: That describes a set.

options.text: Tableau automatically separates date fields into hierarchies.
options.rationale: A date field can be drilled, for example from year to quarter to month.

options.text: A hierarchy removes the rows that fail a condition on a measure.
options.rationale: Removing rows by a condition is the job of a filter.

explanation: A hierarchy organizes related dimensions for drilling. Date fields come with built-in hierarchies. Merging members is a group, In and Out is a set, and removing rows is a filter.

stem: Which two Driftlight requests are best served by a hierarchy? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: Merge the Cologne and Köln spellings of a city into one member.
options.rationale: That is a group.

options.text: Let catalogue staff browse titles by `Type`, then `Genre`, then `Sub-Genre`, expanding only where needed.
options.rationale: Stacked dimensions that are explored from general to detailed are a hierarchy.

options.text: Mark the 20 titles with the most minutes as In and all others as Out.
options.rationale: That is a set.

options.text: Show only sessions that happened on a TV.
options.rationale: That is a filter on `Device`.

options.text: Drill a title report from `Type` down to `Genre` with the + icon, and back up with -.
options.rationale: Drilling up and down is the point of a hierarchy.

explanation: Drilling between levels of detail calls for a hierarchy. Merging spellings is a group, top N by a measure is a set, and restricting rows is a filter.

stem: An analyst drags the `Device` field from the Data pane to the Filters shelf. What happens next?

options.text: The Filter dialog box opens.
options.rationale: When a field is added to the Filters shelf, the Filter dialog opens so you can define the filter.

options.text: A filter card appears on the sheet and the analyst cannot edit the filter.
options.rationale: A card appears only after Show Filter is chosen, and a card lets viewers change the filter.

options.text: The field is added to the view as a discrete header on Rows.
options.rationale: Dropping on Filters does not put the field into the view itself.

options.text: A set named `Device Set` is created automatically.
options.rationale: Sets are made with Create Set or Create > Set; adding a filter creates none.

explanation: Dragging a field to the Filters shelf opens the Filter dialog. The field does not need to be in the view to filter it.

stem: An analyst wants to keep only titles whose names contain the text "Night". Which tab of the dimension filter dialog fits?

options.text: General
options.rationale: The General tab is for ticking individual members, not for matching part of a name.

options.text: Condition
options.rationale: The Condition tab sets a rule on a measure, such as `SUM(Minutes Watched) > 20000`.

options.text: Wildcard
options.rationale: The Wildcard tab matches text, such as names that contain, start with or end with a string.

options.text: Top
options.rationale: The Top tab limits the filter to the top or bottom N members by a measure.

explanation: The four tabs are General (pick members), Wildcard (match text), Condition (a rule on a measure) and Top (top or bottom N by a measure).

stem: The analyst wants a dimension filter that keeps the ten titles with the highest `SUM(Minutes Watched)`. Which tab of the filter dialog defines this?

options.text: General
options.rationale: The General tab only lets you tick members one by one; it can't rank them by a measure.

options.text: Wildcard
options.rationale: The Wildcard tab matches text patterns in member names, not measure rankings.

options.text: Condition
options.rationale: The Condition tab sets a rule such as a minimum, not a count of the highest-ranked members.

options.text: Top
options.rationale: The Top tab keeps the top or bottom N members by a measure.

explanation: The Top tab limits a dimension filter to the top or bottom N members by a measure, for example the top 10 titles by minutes watched.

stem: An analyst drags `Minutes Watched` to the Filters shelf, chooses Sum and clicks Next. The goal is to keep only marks whose summed minutes reach a minimum value. Which option is right?

options.text: Wildcard
options.rationale: Wildcard is a tab of dimension filters; a measure filter offers numeric choices.

options.text: At Least
options.rationale: At Least keeps the marks whose aggregated value is at or above the number entered.

options.text: Special, with Null values
options.rationale: Special only selects null values, non-null values or all values; it sets no minimum.

options.text: Individual dates
options.rationale: That is a choice for date fields, not for a measure.

explanation: A measure filter offers Range of Values, At Least, At Most and Special. It works on the aggregated value of each mark, like `HAVING` in SQL.

stem: A view shows the top 10 titles by minutes watched, filtered with a Top 10 dimension filter. The analyst adds a `Device` filter for TV, but the Top 10 is still computed over all devices. What fixes this?

options.text: Right-click the `Device` filter and choose Add to Context.
options.rationale: A context filter runs before the other dimension filters, so the Top 10 is computed among TV sessions only.

options.text: Change the `Device` filter into a measure filter on `Sessions (Count)`.
options.rationale: Measure filters run after dimension filters, which makes the order problem worse, not better.

options.text: Turn the Top 10 filter into a wildcard filter on the title names.
options.rationale: Wildcard matches text and has no ranking; it would not make the `Device` filter run first.

options.text: Drag the `Device` pill to the Marks card as a detail.
options.rationale: Detail changes the level of detail of the marks; it doesn't change when filters are applied.

explanation: Dimension filters, including Top N, run at the same stage. Add to Context on the other filter makes it run first, and the pill turns gray.

stem: The operations team wants viewers of a dashboard to choose the `Device` themselves, using a control on the sheet. Which step creates it?

options.text: Select the marks and choose Keep Only from the tooltip.
options.rationale: Keep Only filters the view for the author but gives viewers no control.

options.text: Create a fixed set from the `Device` marks and drag it to Rows.
options.rationale: A fixed set never changes and isn't a filter control.

options.text: Add the `Device` field to the Filters shelf and choose the General tab.
options.rationale: That sets the filter for the author; no card is shown until Show Filter is chosen.

options.text: Open the field's drop-down menu and select Show Filter.
options.rationale: Show Filter puts a filter card on the sheet, and its menu sets the mode, such as Multiple Values (Dropdown).

explanation: Show Filter adds a filter card to the sheet so viewers can filter themselves. The card has modes such as Single Value (List) or Multiple Values (Dropdown).

stem: Which two actions add a filter to a view? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: Drag a field to the Filters shelf.
options.rationale: Dropping a field on Filters opens the Filter dialog.

options.text: Drag one field on top of another field in the Data pane.
options.rationale: That creates a hierarchy, not a filter.

options.text: Select marks and choose Exclude from the tooltip.
options.rationale: Keep Only and Exclude both filter the view.

options.text: Click the group icon after selecting headers.
options.rationale: That groups the selected members into one.

options.text: Right-click a mark and choose Create Set.
options.rationale: That creates a set; a set is not a filter by itself.

explanation: Filters are added by dragging a field to the Filters shelf, or by selecting marks or headers and choosing Keep Only or Exclude.

stem: Which two statements about context filters are true? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: They appear at the top of the Filters shelf.
options.rationale: Context filters are listed first on the shelf.

options.text: They run after filters on measures.
options.rationale: They run earlier than dimension and measure filters, not later.

options.text: They are identified by a gray color.
options.rationale: A filter added to context shows as a gray pill.

options.text: They can only be created on date fields.
options.rationale: Any dimension filter can be added to context, not only dates.

options.text: They are applied before extract filters.
options.rationale: Extract filters are the first stage of the order of operations.

explanation: A context filter is created with Add to Context on a dimension filter. It runs before the other dimension filters, shows in gray and sits at the top of the Filters shelf.

stem: Which two kinds of filter does Tableau apply before context filters? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: Extract filters
options.rationale: They are first in the order of operations.

options.text: Filters on dimensions
options.rationale: These run after context filters.

options.text: Filters on measures
options.rationale: These run after dimension filters, so also after context filters.

options.text: Data source filters
options.rationale: They are applied second, right after extract filters.

options.text: Table calculation filters
options.rationale: These are applied last of all.

explanation: The order is extract filters, data source filters, context filters, dimension filters, then measure filters. Table calculation filters are applied last.

stem: A Driftlight operations dashboard must always show the last 30 days, whenever a user opens it. Which kind of date filter fits?

options.text: Range of dates, with a fixed starting and ending date
options.rationale: A fixed range doesn't move; it shows the same days every time the view is opened.

options.text: Date part, with Days selected
options.rationale: A date part keeps specific numbered parts, which doesn't follow the current date.

options.text: Relative dates
options.rationale: A relative date filter updates based on the date and time the view is opened.

options.text: Individual dates, with the last 30 days ticked
options.rationale: Ticked individual dates are fixed and do not move as time passes.

explanation: Relative dates cover a range that updates with the date and time you open the view, such as the last 30 days. A range of dates is fixed.

stem: The analyst needs sessions from 1 January 2025 to 31 March 2025 and nothing else. Which date filter type should they choose?

options.text: Range of dates
options.rationale: It is a fixed range with a starting and an ending date.

options.text: Relative dates, with the last 3 months
options.rationale: Relative dates move with the date you open the view, so they wouldn't stay on this fixed quarter.

options.text: Date part, with Quarters
options.rationale: A date-part filter would keep the same quarter of every year, not one specific range.

options.text: Special, with non-null dates
options.rationale: Special only selects null dates, non-null dates or all dates; it doesn't limit the range.

explanation: A range of dates is "a fixed range of dates" with a start and an end. It is different from a relative date filter, which moves with today's date.

stem: A planner wants to compare every December across all years in the data. Which date filter does this?

options.text: Relative dates, with the last 12 months
options.rationale: This gives one moving 12-month window, not every December of every year.

options.text: Date part, with Months and December selected
options.rationale: A date-part filter keeps the chosen part of every year.

options.text: Range of dates, from 1 December to 31 December
options.rationale: A range of dates includes a year in its start and end, so it can't cover every year's December.

options.text: Special, with all dates
options.rationale: Special with all dates keeps everything, so nothing is filtered.

explanation: A date-part filter picks specific parts, such as certain quarters or months, and applies them to every year in the data.

stem: The team wants all sessions from 1 June 2025 onward, with no end date, so that new data appears later without any change. Which setting fits a range of dates?

options.text: Set both a starting and an ending date, and leave the end at today's date.
options.rationale: The end date would be fixed and new data after it would not appear.

options.text: Choose Individual dates and tick every date since 1 June 2025.
options.rationale: Ticked dates are fixed; later dates are not included automatically.

options.text: Choose Date part with Years and select 2025.
options.rationale: This keeps the whole of 2025, including the months before June.

options.text: Choose a starting date only.
options.rationale: A range of dates can have only a Starting date, leaving the end open.

explanation: A range of dates can be limited by a starting date only or an ending date only, as well as both.

stem: A relative date filter normally counts back from the date and time the view is opened. How can it be changed to count back from a different date?

options.text: It can be set relative to a specific anchor date instead of today.
options.rationale: A relative date filter can be anchored to a chosen date rather than the current date.

options.text: Not at all; relative dates always use today and cannot be changed.
options.rationale: Relative filters can use an anchor date, so this limit does not exist.

options.text: By converting the filter into a context filter first.
options.rationale: Context filters change the order of filtering, not the reference date.

options.text: By switching to a measure filter on the date field.
options.rationale: Measure filters work on aggregated numbers and don't set a reference date.

explanation: A relative date filter works from today by default, but "can also be relative to a specific anchor date rather than today".

stem: Which two choices does Tableau offer when a date field is dragged to the Filters shelf? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: Wildcard match on the date text
options.rationale: Wildcard matching is a tab of dimension filters, not an option for dates.

options.text: Relative dates
options.rationale: A range that updates with the date you open the view.

options.text: Top N by a measure
options.rationale: That is a Top tab choice for dimension filters, not a date filter type.

options.text: Condition on a measure
options.rationale: A condition is a tab of dimension filters, not a date filter type.

options.text: Individual dates
options.rationale: It lets you tick specific dates.

explanation: The date filter dialog offers relative dates, a range of dates, a date part, individual dates and special choices (null, non-null or all dates).

stem: Which two Driftlight requests call for a date-part filter? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: Show only the last 4 weeks, updated each time the dashboard opens.
options.rationale: That is a relative date filter.

options.text: Show only Q4 of each year in the data.
options.rationale: Selecting the Quarters part filters the same quarter of every year.

options.text: Show 1 January to 30 June 2025 only.
options.rationale: That is a range of dates.

options.text: Show only January and February of every year.
options.rationale: A date-part filter on Months keeps those months in every year.

options.text: Show only sessions on a TV.
options.rationale: That is a dimension filter on `Device`.

explanation: A date-part filter keeps specific parts, such as quarters or months, across all years. Moving windows are relative dates and fixed stretches are ranges.

stem: The chart shows `Subscribers (Count)` for each `City`, filtered to one country. Two bars are the same city under different spellings. What should the analyst do so the city appears as one bar?

options.text: Drag `City` to Filters and use Keep Only on the spelling that has more subscribers.
options.rationale: This hides the other spelling's subscribers, so the count for the city is too low instead of combined.

options.text: Select both bars, right-click and choose Create Set, then put the set on Rows.
options.rationale: A set only splits members into In and Out. The two spellings would still be separate members.

options.text: Select both bars or headers and click the group icon, then rename the group.
options.rationale: A group combines the selected members into one, so their subscribers are counted in a single bar.

options.text: Drag `City` onto another field in the Data pane to build a hierarchy from the two spellings.
options.rationale: A hierarchy stacks different fields for drilling. It doesn't merge members of one field.

explanation: Merging members of one field into a bigger category is the job of a group. Select the members in the view and use the group icon (paperclip), or use Create > Group in the Data pane, then rename it.

stem: The analyst selects the Mobile and Tablet headers in this chart and clicks the group icon. Which two statements are true? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: The two members become one mark, and the group's default name is built from the combined member names.
options.rationale: A group combines the selected members into a single group and names it from the member names until it is renamed.

options.text: Selecting Include 'Other' in the Edit Group dialog would gather the remaining members into one more group.
options.rationale: Include 'Other' puts all members that aren't in a named group into one Other group.

options.text: The sessions for Mobile and Tablet are deleted from the data source.
options.rationale: Grouping changes how members are combined in the view. It never removes rows from the data.

options.text: Each session is now marked In or Out of a subset, shown in two colors.
options.rationale: That describes a set. A group makes bigger categories, not an In/Out split.

options.text: The group adds + and - icons so the analyst can drill from the group down to the devices.
options.rationale: Drilling icons belong to hierarchies. A group has no drill path.

explanation: A group merges members into a bigger category and gives it a name. Include 'Other' extends it by lumping every ungrouped member together. The underlying data stays unchanged.

stem: This chart shows `Subscribers (Count)` per `Country`. The head of marketing picks a handful of launch markets by hand. They want those bars colored differently from the rest, and the list must stay the same when new data arrives. What fits?

options.text: Select the launch-market marks, choose Create Set, and put the set on Color as In/Out.
options.rationale: Selecting marks makes a fixed set, and Color shows its In and Out members as two colors.

options.text: Create a dynamic set on the Top tab and put it on Color.
options.rationale: A Top set follows the data and can change members when the numbers change, so the list wouldn't stay fixed.

options.text: Select the launch-market marks and create a group, then put the group on Color.
options.rationale: A group merges the selected countries into one bar. It doesn't keep the other bars separate and compared against them.

options.text: Select the launch-market marks and choose Keep Only, then add the `Country` field to Color.
options.rationale: Keep Only is a filter. It removes the other countries, so there is nothing left to compare against.

explanation: A set marks a subset as In or Out. Made from selected marks it is fixed, so its members don't change when the data does, and its In/Out view on Color compares the subset with the rest.

stem: The `Type`, `Genre` and `Sub-Genre` pills are on Rows, and the chart shows nested headers. What do the nested headers mean?

options.text: Each level is a filter, and only members that pass all three filters are drawn.
options.rationale: The pills are on Rows, not on the Filters shelf. Nested headers split the view; they don't remove marks.

options.text: Each header is a group that was created by combining the members below it.
options.rationale: Groups are created with the group icon or Create > Group. Headers only show the levels placed on a shelf.

options.text: The headers sort the bars, so `Type` is the primary sort and `Sub-Genre` the last.
options.rationale: Sorting is a separate setting. Headers show the structure of the view, not a sort order.

options.text: Each `Sub-Genre` header sits inside a `Genre` header, which sits inside a `Type` header.
options.rationale: Fields placed in order on a shelf nest from general to detailed. This is the drilled-down state of a hierarchy.

explanation: A hierarchy stacks related dimensions from general to detailed. Drilling down adds the next level as nested headers inside the one above, and drilling up removes it again.

stem: The chart shows titles per `Type`. The catalogue team wants to click a + icon on the pill to see the `Genre` break down under each `Type`, without rebuilding the view. What should be set up in the Data pane?

options.text: A group that combines `Type` and `Genre` into one field, placed on Rows.
options.rationale: A group merges members of one field. It doesn't give a field a drill path.

options.text: A hierarchy with `Type` first and `Genre` below it, placed on Rows.
options.rationale: The hierarchy field shows a + icon. Clicking it drills down and adds `Genre` as the next nested header.

options.text: A fixed set that holds every `Genre`, placed on Rows.
options.rationale: A set divides members into In and Out. It doesn't add a drill level.

options.text: A `Genre` filter shown as a filter card on the sheet.
options.rationale: A filter card limits which members are shown. It doesn't add a level of detail.

explanation: Drilling needs a hierarchy. Drop one field on top of another in the Data pane, name the hierarchy, and then use the + and - icons on its pill in the view.

stem: The `Device` pill on Filters excludes Web. `Device` is on no other shelf. What does each bar in the chart show?

options.text: The minutes from Web sessions only, because the excluded member is the one that is drawn.
options.rationale: Exclude removes the ticked members. It doesn't keep them.

options.text: The minutes from all sessions, because a filter on a field that isn't in the view has no effect.
options.rationale: A field doesn't have to be in the view to filter it, so the filter still applies.

options.text: The minutes from sessions on every device except Web, split by `Genre`.
options.rationale: The dimension filter removes the Web sessions before the minutes are summed per genre.

options.text: The minutes for every genre, but genres that have any Web session are removed from the chart.
options.rationale: Filtering removes rows before aggregation. A genre isn't dropped, only its Web sessions are.

explanation: A dimension filter works on rows before they are aggregated. With Exclude selected, the ticked members are removed and everything else stays, even when the filtered field is not in the view.

stem: The shelves show one title per row and a `SUM(Minutes Watched)` filter set to at least 30,000. What does the filter keep?

options.text: Titles whose total minutes across all their sessions reach 30,000.
options.rationale: A measure filter is applied to each mark's aggregated value, after the sessions are summed per title.

options.text: Sessions in which at least 30,000 minutes were watched.
options.rationale: The pill is an aggregate. A filter on single rows would use the unaggregated field.

options.text: The 30,000 titles with the most minutes watched.
options.rationale: That is a Top filter, which counts members. This one compares a value against a threshold.

options.text: Every title, with the bars for smaller titles drawn in gray.
options.rationale: Filters remove marks. They never recolor them.

explanation: A measure filter works on aggregates, like `HAVING` in SQL. Tableau sums the measure for each mark and keeps the marks that pass, so the rule applies to totals and not to single sessions.

stem: The view has a `Device` filter set to TV and a `SUM(Minutes Watched)` filter, with one title per row. Which two statements describe how Tableau applies them? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: The `Device` filter removes the non-TV sessions first, so each title's total counts TV minutes only.
options.rationale: Filters on dimensions run before filters on measures, so the totals are built from TV sessions.

options.text: The `SUM(Minutes Watched)` filter is judged on each title's aggregated value.
options.rationale: A measure filter compares the aggregate of each mark with its rule, after the dimension filter.

options.text: The measure filter runs before the `Device` filter, because measures are calculated first.
options.rationale: The order is fixed: dimension filters, then measure filters.

options.text: The `Device` filter only works if `Device` is also on Rows or Columns.
options.rationale: A filtered field doesn't have to be in the view.

options.text: Both filters are context filters, because they share the Filters shelf.
options.rationale: A filter is only a context filter after Add to Context, and then its pill turns gray.

explanation: Tableau applies filters in a fixed order: extract, data source, context, dimension, then measure filters. So the dimension filter shapes the rows and the measure filter then judges the totals.

stem: The chart shows `SUM(Minutes Watched)` by month, colored by year, and only November and December appear in both years. Which filter on `Start` produced it?

options.text: A range of dates from 1 November 2024 to 31 December 2025.
options.rationale: That range would also keep every month between the two, such as March 2025.

options.text: A relative date filter for the last 2 months.
options.rationale: A relative filter keeps one moving window, so two separate years wouldn't both show.

options.text: A starting date of 1 November 2024, with no end date.
options.rationale: Starting dates keep everything after the date, so the months between would show too.

options.text: A date-part filter on Months with November and December ticked.
options.rationale: A date-part filter keeps the same parts of every year, here both November and December.

explanation: A date-part filter keeps specific parts, such as months or quarters, across all years. Ranges and relative filters keep one continuous stretch of the timeline.

stem: The `Start` pill is continuous (green) on Columns. A second `Start` pill on Filters holds a range of dates from 1 January 2025 to 30 June 2025. Which two statements are true? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: The range keeps one fixed stretch of the timeline, and it doesn't move when the view is opened later.
options.rationale: A range of dates has fixed ends. A relative date filter is the one that moves with the date.

options.text: The pill on Columns draws the timeline, and the pill on Filters decides which dates are kept.
options.rationale: These are two separate pills with different jobs. The one on Columns doesn't filter.

options.text: The filter keeps January to June of every year in the data.
options.rationale: That is a date-part filter on Months. A range keeps only the dates between its two ends.

options.text: The filter updates to the last six months each time the view is opened.
options.rationale: That would be a relative date filter, which counts back from the date the view is opened.

options.text: Placing a continuous date on Columns already limits the view to the dates in the filter.
options.rationale: A pill on a shelf shows what exists in the data. Only the Filters shelf removes dates.

explanation: A range of dates is fixed, a relative date filter moves with the calendar, and a date part repeats across years. A date can be on a shelf and on Filters at once, with separate jobs.

stem: A `Start` filter on this view is a range of dates, 1 July 2024 to 31 December 2024. Next year new sessions are loaded and the analyst opens the view. What does the filter show?

options.text: The latest six months in the data, because Tableau moves date filters forward on its own.
options.rationale: Only a relative date filter moves with the calendar.

options.text: Still 1 July 2024 to 31 December 2024, because the ends of a range are fixed.
options.rationale: A range of dates keeps exactly the stretch it was set to, however much new data arrives.

options.text: Every date from 1 July 2024 to the newest date, because the end follows the data.
options.rationale: That would need a starting date with no end date. This filter has an end date.

options.text: The third and fourth quarters of every year, including the new one.
options.rationale: That describes a date-part filter on Quarters. This one is a single range.

explanation: The ends of a range of dates are fixed. To keep a window that follows the calendar, use a relative date filter; to repeat the same months or quarters each year, use a date-part filter.
